title: Two amateur astronomers use Astra and Codex to search for exoplanets and surface dozens of candidates
summary: You don't need an observatory to join the search. Two amateur astronomers separately used OpenAI's Astra and Codex to comb NASA's public telescope data for signs of exoplanets, then handed their candidates to professional astronomers for follow-up.
ai_summary: OpenAI has published a science case: two amateur astronomers separately used Codex and Astra to search NASA public data for exoplanets. Kevin Bond used Codex to analyze about 100,000 Kepler stars, flagging more than 200 signals, 10 of which are known planets; he narrowed to two priority candidates, one of which dims every 13.8 days and, if caused by a planet, would be about 2.4 times Earth's diameter. Ethan Byrd used Astra to analyze about 19 million stars, surfacing 49 candidates in a first pass; the strongest was sent to TESS for analysis. An astronomer at the SETI Institute independently reviewed the results and found two of the same signals. For now these are candidates only; confirming them as planets could take months or even years.
brief: Two amateur astronomers, separately using Codex and Astra, found exoplanet candidates in public telescope data and have passed them to professional astronomers for review.
Bond searched about 100,000 Kepler stars; the program flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 known planets.
Byrd searched about 19 million stars, surfaced 49 candidates in a first pass, and sent one to the TESS team for analysis.
None of these candidates is confirmed as a planet yet: an independent SETI Institute search found two of Bond's signals, and confirmation could take months or years.

sections.h: What this is: two amateurs use AI to find planet candidates in public data

blocks.p: Since the first exoplanets were announced in 1992, astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system. Amateur astronomers around the world have long been part of that effort: some dig through public telescope data looking for periodic dips in starlight, while others use their own telescopes to watch for the next transit and share what they see with researchers.

OpenAI's case study focuses on two amateurs: Kevin Bond, an OpenAI engineer, and Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure startup Primitive. Working independently, they used different AI tools — Bond used Codex, Byrd used Astra — to analyze public NASA data, found exoplanet candidates, and have handed those leads to professional astronomers for independent assessment.

sections.h: Looking for planets means watching for periodic dips in starlight

blocks.p: The most common way to find exoplanets is the transit method. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view, it blocks a little starlight. On a graph of the star's brightness over time — a light curve — that crossing appears as a dip. If the dip repeats at regular intervals, astronomers know when to look again.

fig.title: A planet passing in front of its star creates a dip in the light curve
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: amber boxes mark the repeated dips — the candidate signal
fig.note: The transit method is one of the most common ways to find exoplanets.

blocks.p: Using AI for this search isn't new. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA's Kepler Space Telescope that astronomers had already examined, teaching it to recognize which starlight patterns were most likely to come from a planet. That model later helped find an eighth planet around the star Kepler-90. The difference here: Bond and Byrd used large models — Codex and Astra — to read the literature, write search programs, and do initial screening, lowering the barrier to entry.

sections.h: Bond's search: two priority candidates from about 100,000 stars

blocks.p: Bond used Codex to search about 100,000 stars observed by the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. He asked Codex to compare published search methods, combine them into a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved results. One AI agent scanned light curves for promising signals; another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first flagged.

fig.title: Bond's search: from about 100,000 stars down to 2 priority candidates
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: amber marks the final priority candidates
fig.note: Ten of the flagged signals come from known planets, used to validate the search method.

blocks.p: The program flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets — finding known planets gave Bond confidence the method could pick out the kinds of signals he was after. Two stars stood out. KIC 5689121 is a relatively cool star about half the size of the Sun in the constellation Lyra; its light curve shows a dip every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing the dip, the blocked light suggests a planet about 2.4 times Earth's diameter. KIC 6691030 is faint in the northern sky and dims every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune.

fig.title: Two priority candidates: one about 2.4 times Earth's diameter, one smaller than Neptune
fig.subtitle: Data from Bond's Kepler search using Codex
rows: Lyra; about half the Sun's size
fig.note: The article's four light curves show the same Kepler observations aligned on a 13.77-day cycle.

blocks.p: An astronomer at the SETI Institute ran an independent search and found the same two signals in the Kepler data. That gives Bond's candidates an external check — but the check only shows the signals are real, not that they are planets.

fig.title: Professional astronomer: this approach can surface candidates traditional searches miss
fig.text: Kevin's work shows how citizen scientists, equipped with AI, can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog—a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler's original targets. His pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed. Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.
fig.role: Associate director for international SETI programs, SETI Institute

sections.h: Byrd's search: 49 candidates from about 19 million stars

blocks.p: Byrd took a different path. He tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars. He used Astra to design two searches: one broad sweep for exoplanet candidates, and another focused on the habitable zone — the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.

The data came from TESS — launched by NASA in 2018 — and other public telescope archives. TESS surveyed both hemispheres in its first 26 sectors, from 2018 to 2020; Kepler watched one field for four years. Byrd asked Astra to read published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. The first pass surfaced 49 candidates: the strongest has been sent to researchers on the TESS mission for follow-up analysis, two more are awaiting submission, and the search is still running.

sections.h: From signal to planet: what's in between

blocks.p: When astronomers see a star dim, they first have to rule out other explanations: two stars passing in front of each other can produce a similar dip, and even temperature changes in a telescope's instruments can make a star appear dimmer. Confirmation requires statistics showing that a planet is the most likely explanation, or follow-up observations with a different method — such as radial velocity, where a planet's gravity tugs on its star, moving it slightly toward and away from us and causing tiny shifts in the color of the star's light.

fig.title: From candidate to confirmed planet: several hurdles remain
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the typical process astronomers use to confirm an exoplanet

steps.name: See periodic dips
steps.desc: The star dims at regular intervals; log it as a candidate.

steps.name: Rule out other causes
steps.desc: Eclipsing binary stars or telescope temperature changes can cause similar dips.

steps.name: Follow up with another method
steps.desc: The planet's gravity makes the star wobble slightly, shifting the color of its light.

steps.name: Publish peer-reviewed findings
steps.desc: Share the evidence so other researchers can check it.

blocks.p: For Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a testable question. If a planet really is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can schedule follow-up for the next transit. More observations can confirm whether the dip repeats on schedule, and additional checks can determine what is actually causing it. OpenAI's article notes that confirming the cause could take months or even years.

sections.h: You can help search for planets without a telescope

list: No telescope: NASA's Exoplanet Watch lets you request data and learn to plot light curves yourself; its citizen science programs offer other ways to participate.
Have a telescope: Exoplanet Watch walks you through collecting transit data and joining observation campaigns.
AAVSO's Exoplanet Observing Program teaches you how to measure a dip in starlight and share your observations with the researchers studying that planet.

The Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets coordinates volunteers around the world who have a certain type of telescope to observe the same star, helping astronomers catch transits that can last longer than a single night.
Price or cost: the article mentions no fees. The searches used NASA public data and OpenAI tools, but it doesn't say what Astra or Codex cost to use, or whether they're free for researchers.
Whether or when the candidates will be confirmed as planets: no answer, only that confirmation could take months or even years.

Other parameters for the planets around the two candidate stars (mass, orbit, atmosphere, whether any is actually in a habitable zone): not provided; the article gives only the period and inferred diameter.
Whether Bond's and Byrd's search programs or code are public: not stated.
How the candidates compare with full professional survey catalogs: it only notes that some signals match known planets, with no full deduplicated list.
How much time the two spent, or how many rounds of AI conversation they used: not stated.

blocks.p: The value of this case study is that it lets AI tools handle part of a job that used to require programming and astronomical training: reading the literature, writing search programs, and doing initial screening. Two amateurs without professional astronomy backgrounds could produce candidates from real public data that professional astronomers can check.

The caveat is just as clear: candidates are not discoveries. Going from a signal to a confirmed planet still involves statistical tests, follow-up observations, and peer review, and could take months or years. This is more like handing leads to professional researchers than announcing a new planet.

list: If you're an astronomy enthusiast who wants to move from stargazing to finding planets in data, start with NASA Exoplanet Watch's public data.
If you can use AI to write code and want a real dataset to practice on, public light-curve archives are an obvious place to start.
If you're introducing students to research, this case is a good way to explain the candidate–verification–confirmation process.
